title: How this site works
preamble: This page explains the rules the platform follows: what a result means, what is counted, and what is public. Opinions on local issues appear only in petitions, attributed to the residents who started them.

definitions.meaning: Residents answer for themselves — on paper, by phone, by text or online — rather than through a poll of a sample. Results here are not binding. Elected officials keep their authority and their responsibility.
Every number cites its source. Every count shows its tier. Every gap is named. The platform’s own books, costs, code and activity log are public.
The platform works alongside the institutions a community already has: its county board, city council and school boards. It is not a replacement for them.

tenets.claim: What the site does and does not do
tenets.evidence: The site computes and cites. Every number links to its source document, and the arithmetic re-adds itself in public. The site does not state opinions, recommend actions or rate officials. Opinions appear only in petitions, attributed to the residents who started them. The site takes no side on candidates, races or ballot measures.

What this project will never do

tenets.evidence: Results here bind no one. Officials keep their authority. A result shows how many people answered, split by verification tier and by channel. When a petition is delivered, the delivery and any official response are recorded on the outcomes page.

Counts are shown as counted and labeled unverified (one per browser) until identity checks are added. All channels go through a single vote path. Names, towns and contact details are kept in a separate private file and never published. When a petition is delivered, its printed copy lists names only for signers who chose to be named. Individual votes are visible to no one.

sources.label: What this project will never do

tenets.claim: How the platform’s own conduct can be checked
tenets.evidence: The activity log is hash-chained and publicly anchored, so a rewrite would show. Visits are counted in the open, with no names or addresses kept. Each announcement to search engines is logged and published. The code is public. Totals re-add themselves on the receipt page. Passwords and encryption protect personal details where the law or safety requires it; the platform’s own conduct is shown and logged rather than hidden behind a lock.

tenets.claim: Where this method has been used
tenets.evidence: New England towns have governed through open town meeting since colonial times. Swiss citizens vote on roughly 15 issues a year, and more than a third of all national referendums ever held worldwide took place in Switzerland. A Stanford study of deliberative polling reported that participants followed politics more closely and voted more nearly a year later. Taiwan’s vTaiwan process used statements people could agree or disagree with but not reply to, and fed rule-making on ride-sharing and online alcohol sales. Porto Alegre, Brazil, was the birthplace of participatory budgeting; a World Resources Institute case study describes improvements there and the later weakening when political commitment faded. Each case is described, with its caveats, on the cases page.

sources.label: The lasting effects of deliberation on civic engagement (Stanford FSI)
Porto Alegre: participatory budgeting and sustaining change (WRI)
Where this has been tried — the cases

tradition.idea: Visiting New England, Tocqueville described town institutions as the schools where liberty is learned — self-government as a practice acquired by doing.

Ostrom’s field research found that communities can govern shared resources without top-down control. Her design principles for institutions that endure include: those affected participate in making the rules; monitoring is done by and answerable to the community; conflict resolution is cheap and accessible; and the community’s right to organize is respected by higher authorities.

Bowling Alone documented two generations of decline in American civic connection — league bowling down 40% while bowling itself rose; meeting attendance, committee service and institutional trust all falling together.

counterarguments.answer: For that reason results here bind no one, and the charter excludes votes on races, active ballot measures, campaigning, and non-elected staff. Questions are about process and money, not about groups of people.

counterarguments.objection: Paid advocacy could try to influence the questions or the counts.
counterarguments.answer: Questions enter through a wording review, and the platform publishes who sponsors it and what it costs.

counterarguments.objection: Voters may lack information on complex questions.
counterarguments.answer: The platform asks few questions, one at a time, each with a plain-language context page linked to cited documents.
For that reason paper ballots at counters, text messaging and kiosks are planned channels, and every result shows its tiers and channels.

counterarguments.objection: Platforms like this can fade when their founders move on.
counterarguments.answer: The code is open, it runs on one inexpensive server, county specifics sit in a single config file, and upkeep is designed to take under three hours a week. Porto Alegre’s participatory budgeting weakened when political commitment faded (WRI case study, above).

counterarguments.objection: Showing how the system works could help bad actors.
counterarguments.answer: Showing how it works lets many people notice a change, a strange count or a bad edit. What stays private is people: no one’s vote, name or address is ever shown.

closing: Opinions on local issues appear only in petitions, attributed to the residents who start them. Everything else on this site is a sourced fact or a computed number.
